newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Mandela arrives to start Angola peace summit.
newsitem.headline: Mandela arrives to start Angola peace summit.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela arrived in Luanda on Wednesday to join regional leaders for a summit to jump-start Angola's troubled two-year-old peace process.

President Jose Eduardo dos Santos met Mandela at the capital's airport where officials said he was to be briefed by the U.N. special envoy to Angola, Alioune Blondin Beye, before heading to a city hotel for the one-day summit.

Heads of state from Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Zambia and Botswana arrived on Tuesday for the meeting but there was no sign by early Wednesday of Jonas Savimbi, the leader of Angola's former rebel movement UNITA.

Regional peacemaker, President Frederick Chiluba of Zambia, had invited Savimbi to join his arch rival dos Santos at the summit with leaders from the 12-nation Southern African Development Community (SADC).
Without him, the effectiveness of the meeting, the first of its kind, will be limited.
There was no word from UNITA as to whether Savimbi, notoriously wary of his physical safety, would come.
The Angolan government and UNITA are implementing a 1994 peace accord to end two decades of civil war.
Southern African leaders are keen to see the peace process completed to ensure stability in the region, but it has slowed almost to a stop.
"We of SADC would want to see the process of peace in Angola proceed much more rapidly than it has been," Zimbabwe President Robert Mugabe told reporters on Tuesday.
"We will look at it and together we will try and find a way of accelerating the process, so there is greater peace and stability in Angola."
Generals from the UNITA army were integrated last month into the national army with their former enemies, but the country remains in practice partitioned and political rapprochement has hardly begun.

Savimbi has rejected the vice-presidency reserved for him under the peace accord. It would have meant moving to government-held Luanda, far away from UNITA headquarters in the northern town of Bailundo.
Peace would dent UNITA's lucrative income from the sale of diamonds mined in areas it controls and would leave the movement playing second fiddle to dos Santos' MPLA.
The MPLA won elections in 1992 after a previous peace accord. UNITA rejected the results and the peace collapsed.
SADC groups Mauritius, Angola, Lesotho, Swaziland, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mozambique, Tanzania, Malawi, Botswana and South Africa.
There was tight security on Luanda's streets before the leaders arrived. Armed soldiers stood on each corner of the major routes.
